get.summary: Lists the designs available to your credentials
get.description:
This route lists the designs you can order, with enough detail to build a picker: each entry carries its faces, themes and preview selections. `GET /v1/designs/{designId}` returns one of those designs in full, adding the attribute categories needed to configure it and create an editor. List first, then fetch the single design your customer chose.

No query parameter is required, but calling the route bare does not list everything. With no `family`, `collection`, `occasion` or `productIds`, the result is restricted to a small configured set of default products -- two flat-card products today -- so a bare call is a sample rather than your catalogue. Send `productIds`, or one of the three filters, to see designs for anything else. `family`, `collection` and `occasion` are mutually exclusive and applied in that order of precedence: `family` beats `collection`, and `collection` beats `occasion`. `occasion` accepts either its id or its slug.

`productIds` takes a comma-separated list of product ids and restricts the list to designs for those products. Every id you send has to resolve to a product that actually appears on the designs this listing returns; one that does not fails the whole request rather than being dropped from the filter. See the 404 note below for what that covers, which is wider than "an id that does not exist".

The response is a flat array of designs, each one carrying the family, occasion and product it belongs to, so a single call has everything needed to group a picker without a second request.

Designs are ordered by their family's priority and then alphabetically by family name. `complexSort=true` inserts recency between those two: families of equal priority whose designs were published more than a day apart are returned newest first, and families published within a day of each other keep the alphabetical order. When you request a `collection`, the order the collection itself defines is used instead and `complexSort` has no effect -- but only when that collection defines its own `designIds`. A master collection, one defined by occasions instead, has no such order to impose and falls back to the family ordering above, where `complexSort` does apply.

A design whose family, occasion or product is not available to your credentials is omitted from the array rather than reported, so a list can be shorter than you expect without anything having failed.

`allowUnpublished=true` is honoured on exactly one listing: a `collection` that defines its own `designIds`. There it returns that collection's unpublished designs alongside the published ones. On an `occasion` listing, and on a bare listing with no filter, it is refused with 400. On a `family` listing it is **ignored** -- the request succeeds and returns published designs only -- and on a master collection, one defined by occasions rather than by an explicit design list, it is refused with 400. Treat a 200 as evidence of nothing: check the designs you got back rather than assuming the flag applied.

`excludeChildCollections` does not control whether nested designs are included; it controls whether a collection that is itself nested inside another can be named at all. It defaults to true, so naming a child collection answers 404 `Collection was not found`. Set it to false to address that child collection directly. Setting it to false while naming a top-level collection changes nothing about the response.

A design, family, collection or occasion that is not available to your credentials returns 404, the same answer as one that does not exist. This is deliberate and is not an authorization failure: the response never reveals whether the thing exists.

The `productIds` 404 is a count check, not an existence check: the request fails whenever the number of products resolved from the returned designs differs from the number of ids you sent. A product you cannot see triggers it, and so does a product you can see that has no design in this particular listing, a disabled product, and the same id sent twice. There is no partial result -- the designs for the ids that did resolve are not returned either. Confirming each id against `GET /v1/products` is necessary but not sufficient, because a valid product with no design here fails the same way.

Design ids come from this list: it is where an integration discovers what it can offer, and the ids it reports are the ones the design detail route accepts.

Call this at the start of an integration, and again whenever your credentials change, to learn exactly which operations your presented token can currently reach -- no separate documentation lookup or support request needed.

Requires only a valid bearer token. No other setup: the response is derived live from your token's scopes, not from a static list that can drift out of date.

The response lists this endpoint alongside every other operation your token admits -- discovery does not omit itself. An operation appearing here means your credential's scopes admit it at the route-authorization layer; it does not guarantee the call will succeed. See the response's own `semantics` array for the complete, load-bearing statement of what a listed operation does and does not promise.

A missing or malformed bearer token returns 401. A well-formed token whose scopes do not admit this operation returns 403. The response is never cached by an intermediary (`Cache-Control: private, no-store` on every status code), since it describes the caller who presented it.

get.summary: Lists the designs available for your products
get.description:
The design catalog is in preview: its request and response shape may change before general availability.

Requires `products` -- a comma-separated list of up to 50 references, each an id, a slug, or a marketing slug, the same references `GET /v1/products` accepts. Also requires `tags` -- a comma-separated list of one or more published tags, matched exactly against the values designs are tagged with. A design must carry every requested tag. Both parameters are required; there is no unfiltered listing.

Each design reports every one of your requested products it applies to, so one call covers several sizes and you can filter your grid without a second request.

A folded card also lists the flat card designs that can be printed folded, and those designs report the folded card among the products they apply to. A flat design that cannot be printed folded is listed only under the flat card.

Each design also reports its colourways, and each one carries its own full-size preview image, taken from the same view as the design's main preview -- so a colourway picker can swap the image without another request. Each colourway also carries a small preview image sized for a swatch picker, so building a swatch strip does not mean pulling ten full-size images. A colourway with no image of its own reports its previews as `null`; both keys are always present. For every layout and every colourway of one design, fetch that design on its own.

Each colourway also carries `swatchHex`, the hex colour of its swatch, so a colour chip needs no second request. Each design reports `photoCounts` -- the fewest and the most photos it can hold, for a label such as "1-6 Photos" -- and `foil`, keyed by each of its `productIds`: `pressed` when the design ships with foil or requires it, `available` when foil can be added, `none` when the product offers none. `displayName` names a design that is a variant of its family as `Family (Variant)`; `name` is `null` when the design has no name.

A reference naming a product you cannot order (invisible to your account, though it exists) contributes no designs and is not an error, because the answer to a multi-product request is the union of what you can actually sell. A request naming only such references returns an empty list with a 200. A reference that matches several of your products, by contrast, is ambiguous and fails the whole request with a 400 naming it -- it is never resolved to a union.

Results default to a curated order: designs are shown in the order defined for the most specific match to your requested `tags`, followed by any remaining matching designs ordered by the name your customer sees. When no curated order is available for your `tags`, results fall back to that same name order on their own -- the name comes from the design family rather than the design itself, so a page may split a family across a boundary, and a design's own `name` may be `null` (the key is always present). The `ordering` field on the response always names which of the two was actually applied. Ordering is stable for identical requests; it is not a snapshot, so a design added or renamed between pages can shift. `totalCount` is the count at the time the page was built.

Paging is by opaque cursor. Follow `nextCursor`; its absence means the last page. A cursor is only valid for the exact `products`, `tags` and `sort` that produced it, AND for the same curated ordering it was minted under -- reusing one after any of those changed (including a curated order changing, or a request flipping between curated and its fallback) is rejected rather than silently re-anchored, and a cursor older than 24 hours is rejected as expired. Cursors are at most 1KB, `limit` may not exceed 200 (default 50), and paging backwards is not supported.

An unrecognised `tags` value is rejected rather than ignored, so a typo fails at integration time instead of returning an empty grid you might mistake for "no designs". Tags are matched exactly against the published values -- there is no alternative-spelling resolution.

get.summary: Lists the products your organization can sell
get.description:
Returns the products your organization can sell, as an envelope: { products: [...], totalCount, nextCursor? }. Products you cannot sell are INVISIBLE rather than forbidden -- they are absent from the list and absent from totalCount, so the count never hints at products arranged for another partner.

Each row is addressed by `ref`, a readable slug rather than an internal id that changes whenever WHCC re-sources a product behind the scenes. Pass `ref` back to every other endpoint. `ref` is caller-relative, not globally unique: where a product is restricted to your organization, it wins the reference for you and the general product wins it for everyone else. When two products TIE for a ref -- both general, or both restricted to you -- this list keeps the first in sort order rather than erroring, but the detail route treats that same tie as ambiguous and answers 400. A ref you see listed here is not guaranteed to resolve on the detail route.

Each row also carries `kind` -- what sort of thing the product is -- and `completion`, who supplies the order content: `api` means you can finish the product headlessly, `editor` means a person must finish its design in a WHCC editor. `kind` is a closed but ADDITIVE-ONLY set: new members may appear over time and existing members never change meaning, so treat a value you do not recognize as "a product I do not handle" rather than as an error. It describes the product for display and routing; order on `ref`.

Geometry reads together. `width` and `height` are the finished size in inches and are present or absent as a pair; when they are absent, `sizedBy` names the configuration fields that determine the size, so the geometry depends on a choice you have not made yet rather than being missing data. `aspect` is the product's derived shape and can read `square`, which is why it is a separate word from the `orientation` you may SEND when configuring. `quantity` carries the ordering constraint -- flat cards, for instance, are min 25 / max 5000 / step 5 -- and all three of `min`, `max` and `step` are enforced when you order.

Every row carries `actions.detail`, the URL to fetch that product in full. It is the one action in this API with no `instructions`: fifty rows repeating one identical sentence about a GET to a URL the row already names would cost you a third of the page in tokens for nothing. Follow the URL rather than building one.

Paging is by cursor, not offset. Ask for up to 200 rows with `limit` (default 50); when more remain you receive `nextCursor`, which you pass back as `cursor`. `nextCursor` is ABSENT on the final page, never null. Cursors are opaque, at most 1024 characters, expire after 24 hours, and are bound to the filters that minted them -- changing `category` or `q` mid-walk is rejected rather than silently re-anchored. Backward paging is not supported.

Results are ordered by name, with an internal tiebreaker that makes the order total. No skipped or duplicated products are guaranteed only while the underlying catalogue is unchanged; a product renamed or withdrawn mid-walk falls under that caveat. Responses are cached for five minutes, which is what `Cache-Control: private, max-age=300` reports. It is `private` because this page is not the same for every caller -- what you can sell, and `totalCount` with it, depend on who you are -- so it must not be held in a cache shared between callers. Error responses (status 400 and above) carry `Cache-Control: private, no-store` instead, so a refusal is never reused after the cause is fixed.

Filter with `category` (exact match on a row's `category.ref`, an opaque token -- compare it, do not parse it) and `q` (case-insensitive substring match on the product name). Neither is required.

A 400 covers an unknown query parameter, an out-of-range `limit`, a malformed or forged cursor, and a cursor whose sort or filters do not match this request. A cursor older than 24 hours is a 410 -- start the walk again without a cursor. Two products sharing a ref never fault this route: the more specific one wins the row (see above), and a tie is resolved silently rather than refused. The detail route is stricter about the same collision -- there, where you named the reference yourself, it can still answer 400 naming the candidates it could not choose between.

post.summary: Create a cart
post.description:
You can create the cart empty and add items with POST .../items afterward, or supply an items[] array here to create the cart and its items together in one transaction -- same per-item shape and the same 1-100 cap as POST .../items.

Your credentials must carry an account identity of the form whcc_ (an API-key token's bound account, or a first-party token's accountId claim); without one the request is rejected with 400. accountId may be omitted and defaults to that identity.

salesChannel is optional and records where the buyer is shopping: { type, id } for an external place of sale (type external; id is your own identifier), or { type, id, linkId } for a share link (type collaborationShare; id is the share id and linkId is required). It is set here and cannot be changed afterward. For collaborationShare the share link must belong to your account and be neither revoked nor expired, and id must be the share that link belongs to. A cart created without salesChannel carries no salesChannel key in any response.

priceBasis is optional and says which price the cart's lines are charged at: wholesale or retail. It is the cart's default; an item's own priceBasis wins over it. Both are set at add or create and cannot be changed afterward. A line's effective basis is its own, else the cart's, else wholesale; nothing fills either in, so a cart or item created without one carries no priceBasis key in any response. retail needs a rule source to price from, which today means a collaborationShare salesChannel. In this release the basis is recorded and carried onto the order at submit; it does not yet change the charged price.

shipping.returnAddress is optional and sets the return address printed on the shipping label of a drop-ship order: { name, addr1, city, state, zip, country } plus optional addr2 and phone. country must be US and phone, if sent, is exactly 10 digits. It maps to the legacy ShipFromAddress, only the shipping label changes (not packing slips, inserts or emails), and it is not allowed with studio shipping. If you ship from outside the US, leave it out and the label carries your account address. A returnAddress of null is ignored.

If accountId is supplied and your credentials already carry an account identity, it must match exactly -- a near-miss value is treated as a mismatch, not normalized. metadata absent or null means an empty map. Guidance and actions are always computed on the response, even for a cart created with no items, so you learn immediately whether it is already submit-ready.

A 400 covers a metadata bounds violation, a malformed item input, an inline item carrying neither editorId nor configuredProductId, more than 100 inline items, an unsupported expand value, a malformed salesChannel (unknown type, external with a linkId, collaborationShare without one, or an unknown key), or a priceBasis other than wholesale or retail (on the cart or an inline item), or a malformed shipping.returnAddress (a non-US country, a phone that is not 10 digits, a missing required field, an unknown key, or any return address on a studio cart) -- a bad item creates neither the cart nor any item. A 403 means accountId was supplied and did not match your credentials' own account identity. A 422 with code cart.salesChannel.invalid means a collaborationShare salesChannel did not resolve: no share link matches linkId in your account, id is not the share that link belongs to, or the share or link is revoked or expired. post.summary: Creates a priced draft from configured products
post.description:
Use this to build editors from product selections and images (partner-hosted URLs, or images you have already uploaded and hold an `imageId` for) and price them in one call. Nothing is submitted here: this route always creates a priced draft, and placing the order is a separate call to POST /v1/commerce/submissions, which the response points you at through `actions.submit`. If you already hold editor IDs, call POST /v1/commerce/submissions directly instead.

Every configured product must reference a product this route can create: one finished through the API, or a card or album your customer finishes in the editor (each of those returns `awaiting-editor`). A card needs a `designId`; an album must not send one. A request is either all products finished through the API or all products finished in the editor, never a mix. A product this route cannot create is rejected before any gallery, image, or editor side effect.

201 means the request supplied an already-uploaded `imageId` for every configured product and no item is still processing. Every other outcome is 202 -- most commonly after submitting partner-hosted image URLs, which are exchanged for images that finish processing asynchronously -- with an otherwise structurally identical response.

Items carry no editor link, and this request takes no `redirects`: where your customer returns after editing is sent with the edit-link request, not here. To let a customer edit an item, request one with `POST /v1/commerce/configured-products/{configuredProductId}/edit-link`. The response root carries one next-step action -- `actions.submit` (targeting `POST /v1/commerce/submissions`) once every item is ready, together with `actions.calculate` (targeting `POST /v1/commerce/submissions/calculate`) to price that order first without placing it, `actions.poll` while any item is still processing, or `actions.fix` if any item failed. Follow `actions.poll.url` (a `GET /v1/commerce/configured-products` request) to check progress; it never creates anything, so call it as often as you like.

For a partner credential, the selection keys you may send are exactly the ones that product's `configuration.fields[]` publishes in the catalog; anything else is a 400 naming the field rather than a key quietly discarded. `selections.quantity` is the exception -- it is a request field of its own -- and it is validated against all three of the product's published `min`, `max` and `step`, with the step counted up from the minimum. A configuration-resolution call gives you both answers without creating anything.

For a custom size, send `dimensions` as `{ "width": w, "height": h }` together with `size: "custom"`, long side as `height`. A box sent without `size: "custom"`, with the width larger than the height, outside the product's published envelope, or ruled out by your other selections is a 400 naming `configuredProducts.{index}.selections.dimensions`. An accepted box is priced at the nearest orderable size at or above it on both axes, while the exact dimensions you sent are what gets made.

404 covers an unresolvable product reference, an unresolvable gallery, or an unresolvable image. 400 covers a malformed payload (including a `redirects` field, which this route does not accept), a product that exists but is not simple-editor compatible, a quantity outside its constraint, a custom size that cannot be made, and a selection key that product does not publish; send only what GET /v1/catalog/products/{ref}'s `configuration.fields[]` lists.

get.description:
Returns one design in full: every face and its layout, the family theme set, and both the attribute categories that configure the design and the order attribute categories that accompany it. Fetch it for the single design a customer has chosen; use `GET /v1/designs` to build the grid they choose from.

Takes a design id exactly as `GET /v1/designs` reports it. There is no alternative identifier: a family name or an occasion slug is not accepted here.

The optional `designVersionIds` pins particular face versions: a JSON object keyed by node id, whose values are the face version ids to serve. The same thing can be sent one face at a time as `designVersionIds.=`, and `designVersionId=` is shorthand for the default node of a single-node design. Any other query parameter is rejected with 400 rather than ignored.

The optional `productId` serves the design against a different product from the one it was drawn for -- this is how a flat card design is previewed as a folded one. Dimensions, faces and attribute categories come back transformed for the product you named. The transformation is ephemeral: it changes nothing about the design itself, and the same design fetched without `productId` is unchanged. A design eligible for this treatment says so in its `metadata.tags`, and the response reports whether a transformation was actually applied.

Naming a `productId` that the design was already drawn for, or another product of the same kind, returns the design untransformed rather than failing -- so passing the product you intend to order is always safe.

A design, family, collection or occasion that is not available to your credentials returns 404, the same answer as one that does not exist. This is deliberate and is not an authorization failure: the response never reveals whether the thing exists.

A `productId` that does not exist returns 400 rather than 404, because you named it explicitly; a product that exists but is not a legal target for this design also returns 400, naming the reason it was refused. A `designVersionIds` value that is not valid JSON is a 400 as well.

A design is readable here when the product it was drawn for is one your credentials can order, so a valid id for a product outside your catalog returns 404.

With an API key, a design that is no longer published also returns 404. Designs are retired over time, so an id saved from an earlier `GET /v1/designs` can stop resolving: treat the 404 as final for that id and drop it from any cached catalog rather than retrying.

get.summary: Gets one product in full, including its configuration model
get.description:
Returns one product in full: every field the list carries, plus `configuration` -- everything you must decide before you can order it. The response is a bare object, not the { products: [...] } envelope the list returns. There is no query parameter to ask for the configuration; it always ships, because the callers least likely to pass one are the agents and headless clients that need it most.

Address the product by `ref`. A product id or slug also works, so whichever identifier you hold resolves. A reference that matches nothing is a 404 -- and so is a product your organization cannot sell, deliberately and identically, so you learn nothing about other organizations' catalogues. A reference that matches more than one product you can see is a 400 naming the candidates and the identifier that separates them; it is never answered by silently picking one.

The product fields are the same ones the list carries. `kind` is what sort of thing the product is and `completion` is who supplies the order content -- `api` if you can finish it headlessly, `editor` if a person must finish its design in a WHCC editor. `kind` is a closed but ADDITIVE-ONLY set: new members may appear and existing members never change meaning, so treat a value you do not recognize as "a product I do not handle" rather than as an error. Where `width` and `height` are absent, `sizedBy` names the configuration fields that decide the size.

`configuration.fields[]` is the UNCONDITIONAL view: the full domain of every field, whatever any particular selection would make applicable. Each field carries a `field` code you send back under `selections`, a display `name`, a baseline `required`, an optional `default`, and a `kind`. What is allowed GIVEN the choices you have made -- and what a configuration costs -- comes from `actions.resolveConfiguration`, never from this response. That action appears only when your key is enrolled in the configuration-resolution preview.

Branch on each field's own `kind`, which is a different word from the product's `kind` above and has its own two values. `enum` carries `values[]` of { id, name, enabled } -- render a dropdown, and grey out anything with `enabled: false`. A size value also carries `width` and `height` in inches, so you can show a customer what they are choosing. `dimension` carries `unit` and `constraints` and NO `values[]`, because its domain is continuous -- render two number inputs and validate against the envelope. `kind` is additive-only: treat one you do not recognize as a field you cannot render, not as an error.

Where a product takes a custom size, you get an envelope rather than a thousand enumerated rows: `width` and `height` bounds that admit either axis as the longer one. Send `{ "width": w, "height": h }` as `dimensions` inside `selections`, together with `size: "custom"`; a 20x16 piece is landscape and a 16x20 piece is portrait, and we derive `orientation` from whichever one you sent, the same way we already derive it from your photo when you omit it. Send `orientation` too only if you want to state it explicitly -- it must then agree with `dimensions`. There is no step within the envelope, but being inside it is necessary, not sufficient: other selections can narrow what is actually orderable, so `actions.resolveConfiguration` is the authority on what will be accepted. What it accepts is priced at the nearest size at or above it.

The published envelope is STATIC -- what is possible for the product at all. Other selections can narrow it, so a value inside the envelope is not yet a value you can order; `actions.resolveConfiguration` (present when your key is enrolled in the configuration-resolution preview) reports the narrowed bounds for the choices in hand.

Some fields in this list are not product attributes at all -- `orientation` is the standing example. They are published here because everything you may send is described in exactly one place, and because you have no other way to learn the key exists. `orientation` in particular appears only on products where it changes something: a product whose sizes are all square, or whose orientation is part of the product you chose, does not offer it.

This list is also the list of selection keys you may SEND. A key this product does not publish is rejected with a 400 naming the field, rather than accepted and silently discarded -- so a misspelling costs you one error instead of an order that quietly omits what you asked for. The rule is the same at `actions.resolveConfiguration` and at the create endpoint, so a payload that resolves cleanly is not refused at order time. A field published here is never reported back to you as unrecognized.

Shipping is not here -- you get it from the order API, where it belongs. Neither are per-face geometry or node data: the create path takes one image placement, so there is nothing a face id would let you do.

Responses are cached for five minutes, which is what `Cache-Control: private, max-age=300` reports -- `private` because the response depends on who is asking, so it must not be held in a cache shared between callers. Error responses (status 400 and above) carry `Cache-Control: private, no-store` instead, so a refusal is never reused after the cause is fixed.

put.summary: Sets the markup on a share
put.description:
targetId is the share id (collaborationShareId on the share-link routes), not a share link id. A share that does not exist and a share belonging to another account both return 404 with the same response -- this is deliberate and does not confirm which case occurred.

Only the share level (level = share) can be used for now. This is a limit of this release, not a rule about where a markup may be set: each other level will be turned on separately. Any other known level returns 422 with code retail_pricing.level.not_writable on PUT, GET and DELETE alike, before anything is looked up. An unknown level returns 400.

The body is a markup rule. A percent rule is { type: "percent", value } where value is basis points in whole percents (700 is 7%), above zero and at most 100000 (1,000%). The wholesale rule { type: "wholesale" } prices the share at cost: it is stored like any other rule and reported as at cost, and it is never checked against the minimum because at cost owes no service fee. Omitted fixed fields (appliesTo, currency, scope, rounding) take their only supported value, and a different value is rejected. One row is kept per share: a second PUT replaces the first.

A percent rule is checked against the share's minimum markup, in basis points. The minimum is the highest, across the share's allowed products, of the smallest whole percent at which one unit of the product nets at least one cent after the service fee, taking the highest across the product's quantity breaks (the minimum is not the same at every price). When the share allows every product (an empty allowed list), the products are the card products. The answer carries the minimum as minimumPercent; for a wholesale rule it is null, because it was not computed.

The minimum is checked again when prices are calculated. A saved percent rule that has fallen below its minimum since the save (costs rose) is still charged as saved, and only logged.

A 400 carries the code of the rule problem (retail_pricing.rule.type_unknown, retail_pricing.rule.unknown_field, retail_pricing.rule.percent_value_not_integer, retail_pricing.rule.percent_value_not_positive, retail_pricing.rule.percent_value_not_whole_percent, retail_pricing.rule.percent_value_above_maximum, and the other retail_pricing.rule codes for a field that is present but unsupported). A 422 with code retail_pricing.rule.below_minimum means a percent rule is under the share's minimum; minimumPercent is in the body and nothing is stored. A 422 with code retail_pricing.input.no_profitable_markup means a product on the share is priced so low that no markup up to 1,000% nets a cent, so no percent rule can be saved. A 422 with code retail_pricing.minimum.unavailable means none of the share's candidate products could be priced (for example every listed product is unknown or not visible to you), so there is no minimum to check against; candidates in the body is how many were tried. Nothing is stored. A wholesale rule can still be saved.

post.description:
Call this to prepare a canonical create item and check its selections before ordering. Nothing is created. `{ref}` is the reference GET /v1/catalog/products gave you, and the URL is the one that product's `actions.resolveConfiguration` names.

Send `quantity` at the top level or inside `selections`; the top-level value wins. If omitted, the product default applies, falling back to 1. The item price excludes shipping, tax, packaging and discounts, so do not display it as an order total.

It is a price, not a frozen quote: it is recomputed on every request, so re-check before you charge a customer.

A syntactically valid request returns 200 with `createItem`, `canCreate`, `price`, and any blockers in `issues[]`. Price is null when the configuration cannot be priced soundly. A price can still be available when design, image, or workflow prerequisites block creation.

Every issue names an actionable selection or prerequisite. Quantity issues name `quantity`. Quantity is checked against the product's published `min`, `max` and `step`; a product at min 25 / step 5 allows 25, 30, 35.

For a custom size, send `dimensions` as `{ "width": w, "height": h }` together with `size: "custom"`. Either axis may be the longer one -- a 20x16 canvas is landscape and a 16x20 canvas is portrait -- and we derive `orientation` from whichever you sent. Send `orientation` yourself only to state it explicitly; it must then agree with `dimensions`, or the request is refused. A box we cannot make is reported as an `invalid_selection_value` issue on `selections.dimensions` -- sent without `size: "custom"`, outside the published envelope, or ruled out by your other selections -- and in every one of those cases `price` is null. `price.pricedAs` names the canonical size the price was actually looked up at, and appears only when that differs from the box you sent.

Send only the selection keys this product's `configuration.fields[]` publishes, plus numeric `selections.quantity` if desired. An unpublished selection key receives a 400 naming that key.

This foundation preview cannot yet validate design or image inputs. Known design and image requirements block creation, as do selection changes to workflow until workflow resolution is supported.

post.description:
The cart must be ready to submit: a shipping address carrying every field WHCC requires, at least one active item, and no active item whose account identity is present but blank. There is no partial submit -- every active item in the cart is ordered -- so move any item you do not want submitted out of the cart first with POST .../move. Soft-removed items are neither submitted nor counted toward readiness.

The body is optional, and absent for an ordinary submit -- all order intent already lives on the cart. The one exception is { paymentData }, for a cart paid before it is submitted (see the next paragraph). No Idempotency-Key header is needed: the server derives its own idempotency key from the cart's id and its assembled-payload checksum, so a caller-sent Idempotency-Key header is accepted but unused. Retrying an already-submitted cart returns the original response again, even if you present a different key on the retry. If-Match is honored (an optional numeric version) and is checked before any Basic Order work runs; the underlying submitting claim is always pinned to the cart's version whether or not If-Match was sent.

Prepaid submit: send { paymentData } (the Basic Order paymentData shape) to mark the order prepaid. paymentProcessor must be Stripe and transactionID must be a Stripe PaymentIntent id (pi_...; a charge id, ch_..., is a 400). The caller needs the order:payments.override scope (403 without it, before any cart work), and prefer=respond-async is refused with a body (400): money has been taken, and the async path answers 202 even when it fails to enqueue. Before the order is placed, Prospector fetches the PaymentIntent from Stripe and requires its metadata.cartId to name this cart; set it when you create the PaymentIntent. That check is always on, and is separate from payment verification. For a prepaid submit the charge id is the idempotency key: retrying the same charge on the same cart never places a second order, and Idempotency-Key is not read. A different charge on an already-submitted cart is a 409, not a replay. paymentData is never returned: not in the response, not in a replay, not in expand=submission. Codes: 422 cart.submit.payment_not_for_cart (the PaymentIntent is not stamped for this cart, or does not exist; not retryable, the cart stays active), 502 cart.submit.payment_unverifiable (Stripe could not be reached; retry, the cart stays active), 409 cart.submit.payment_already_submitted (the cart was already submitted without this charge) and 409 cart.submit.payment_already_used (this charge already paid for another order; the cart stays active).

A 400 covers a malformed cartId or prefer value, an invalid paymentData, a malformed If-Match header (a single numeric version, optionally quoted; "*" is not supported), or a cart holding a shipping.returnAddress whose shipping is studio. A cart that does not exist and a cart belonging to another tenant both return 404 with the same response -- this is deliberate and does not confirm which case occurred. Credentials that do not carry an account identity of the form whcc_ are rejected with the same 400 on every cart route. A 409 means the cart is soft-deleted (restore it first), currently submitting (a prior submit is in flight or awaiting operator repair, code cart.lifecycle.submit_in_flight), or the supplied (or underlying) version no longer matches the stored one -- both version cases carry currentVersion so you can refetch and retry. A 422 means the cart is not ready to submit; invalidParams enumerates every gap at once, each entry carrying the registered code for that gap alongside its reason, and the cart is left untouched and stays mutable.

Omitting it is NOT last-write-wins on this route -- the submitting claim is version-pinned to the cart this request read either way, so a concurrent mutation loses the claim rather than letting a stale payload be ordered. Ignored on an already-submitted cart, where the idempotent short-circuit answers first.

post.summary: Mints a fresh edit link for a configured product
post.description:
Call this to give your customer a link to edit an item, and again whenever the link you already have has expired -- links expire after 30 days -- or was simply lost. Every call mints a brand new link.

Pass the item's `configuredProductId` exactly as you received it, in the URL path. It is opaque -- do not decode or reconstruct it. Send `redirects` in the body: `redirects.complete` and `redirects.cancel` are both required. `complete` is the link your customer returns to when they finish editing; `cancel` is where the editor's exit button sends them when they leave without finishing. `redirects.secondary` is optional. Each link is `{ "text": "...", "url": "https://..." }`; the url must be https. Any other key, such as `done` or `locked`, is a 400.

Each call stores these links on the item, replacing any it had. The last call wins, including for links you minted earlier: they open the same item, so they use the links stored most recently. Simple items created by the same request share one editor, so the links apply to all of them; a card or album has its own. WHCC default links are never added. To tell which item came back, put your own key (for example your order id) in the url. For a card or album, `%EDITOR_ID%` in a url becomes that item's `configuredProductId`, and `guidance` tells you when `redirects.complete` has no such marker.

Optionally send `settings` to configure the editor, each one `true` or `false`: `hidePricing` and `disableUploads` (`true` hides prices, or hides the photo upload control without blocking uploads), and `productSwitcher`, `sizeSelector`, `quantitySelector`, `wallArrangement`, `multiProduct`, `addToProject` and `presentationMode` (`true` shows or turns on that control). Settings are stored on the item like the links, and the last call that sends `settings` wins: a setting it leaves out goes back to the default, and `settings: {}` resets them all. A call without `settings` leaves the stored settings as they are. `hidePricing` is the exception: it applies to the link this call returns, unless your customer adds the item to a project that sets its own pricing visibility. Each editor uses only the settings it has: a simple item uses all of them; an album uses all but `quantitySelector`, `wallArrangement` and `multiProduct`; a card uses `hidePricing`, `disableUploads`, `addToProject` and `presentationMode`. A setting the editor does not have is accepted and has no effect.

The link opens the whole design space this configured product belongs to, not a link scoped to just this one configured product -- if the design space holds more than one, all of them are reachable from the same link.

A design space that has already been submitted may no longer accept edits; this route still issues a link regardless, since whether editing is currently possible is a property of the design space, not of this call.

The returned URL is a bearer credential for editing the design space -- do not cache, log, or share it beyond the person who will use it.

404 covers both an unrecognized `configuredProductId` and one that belongs to a different caller -- the two are indistinguishable by design; nothing is stored in either case. 400 covers a missing body, a missing `redirects.complete` or `redirects.cancel` (both are named when both are missing), a url that is not https, any key other than `complete`, `cancel` and `secondary`, a setting that is not `true` or `false`, and any setting not listed above (the error names it); nothing is stored in that case either. If minting fails with a 5xx, the links and settings you sent may already be stored; call again.

post.summary: Move a cart item to another cart (the named-cart workflow primitive, e.g. current ↔ saved-for-later)
post.description:
The named-cart workflow primitive -- for example, moving an item between a "current" cart and a "saved for later" cart -- without losing the item's id, label, timestamps, or removed state, which a remove-then-re-add would not preserve.

targetCartId must differ from cartId and must share the source cart's accountId.

The item's id, label, timestamps and removed state are preserved across the move -- a removed item moves and stays removed. Both carts' versions are bumped in the same transaction. expand=cart returns the TARGET cart, not the source. An item with its own priceBasis of retail cannot move into a cart with no collaborationShare salesChannel (422); an item without its own priceBasis moves freely and still carries none.

A 400 covers a malformed targetCartId, targetCartId equal to cartId (self-move), a malformed cartId/itemId, a malformed If-Match header, or an unsupported expand value. A 422 with code cart.priceBasis.noRuleSource means the item's own priceBasis is retail and the target cart has no collaborationShare salesChannel. A 404 means no source cart, no target cart, or no item was found -- identical for a nonexistent resource and one belonging to another tenant. For account-bound callers, including API-key callers, a target cart under a different account also returns 404. A 409 means either the usual lifecycle/version conflict on the source cart, the target cart's own lifecycle status doesn't permit the move, or the move would put the TARGET cart over its 500-active-item limit (only an active item consumes the target's budget).

code.description:
Stable automation contract; a retired code is never reused. Known codes and their meanings:
- `order.lifecycle.staged` -- The order has been accepted and validated but has not reached fulfillment; its status becomes order_placed only after submission to WHCC succeeds.
- `order.lifecycle.submission_enqueued` -- The order was accepted for asynchronous submission; the response status is optimistic and placement has not been confirmed yet.
- `order.correlation.order_id` -- `id` is this order's permanent identifier. Use it to look the order up and to match it to your own records.
- `order.correlation.confirmation_pending` -- WHCC order numbers are assigned after submission and aren't available yet. Use `id` until they appear.
- `order.support.cancellation_via_fulfillment` -- This route does not cancel orders. To cancel a placed WHCC order, call POST /api/v1/fulfillment/orders/{id}/cancel-actions, then POST /api/v1/fulfillment/orders/{id}/cancellation with the cancelToken it returns; {id} is the fulfillment order id or WHCC order number. Whether an order can still be canceled is in its cancelEligibility on GET /api/v1/fulfillment/orders/{id}.
- `order.safe_use.result_ordering_unspecified` -- Result ordering is not guaranteed; correlate results by configuredProductId.
- `product.correlation.reference_resolved` -- A product slug or marketingSlug was resolved to a specific product; productId in this response is the resolved product and is the stable reference. Slug resolution is scoped to your credentials, so the same slug may resolve to a different product for another caller.
- `webhook.support.registration_unavailable` -- Webhook registration is not available to API-key integrations; WHCC configures callback URIs during partner onboarding. Contact your WHCC integration contact to have a callback URI registered for your account.
- `cart.items.limit_exceeded` -- A cart cannot hold more than the maximum number of active items; remove items from the cart, or use a different cart, before adding, restoring or moving items into it.
- `cart.submit.shipping_address_missing` -- This cart's shipping address is missing required fields: name, addr1, city, state, zip. Submit will be rejected until they are set.
- `cart.submit.items_missing` -- This cart has no active items; submit will be rejected until at least one is added.
- `cart.submit.account_identity_missing` -- One or more active items are missing account identity; submit will be rejected until each item either carries a valid whccAccountId or is updated to allow the cart's own account to apply.
- `cart.items.contains_removed` -- This cart contains soft-removed items; they are excluded from pricing, submit and default listings, and do not affect readiness to submit.
- `cart.lifecycle.submitted` -- This cart has already been submitted as an order and is now read-only.
- `cart.lifecycle.deleted` -- This cart has been soft-deleted; restore it before it can be modified or submitted.
- `cart.lifecycle.submit_in_flight` -- A submit for this cart is being processed; the cart is temporarily read-only until it completes or is repaired.
- `cart.item.unresolvable` -- One or more items reference an editor that could not be found, so no order preview could be generated for this cart.
- `order.fanout.multiple_whcc_orders` -- A single order can be split into more than one WHCC order; each has its own order number and confirmation id and ships and tracks independently. Do not assume a one-to-one mapping between an order and a WHCC order.
- `submission.fanout.multiple_orders` -- A single submission can be split into more than one WHCC order; each has its own order number and confirmation id and ships and tracks independently. Do not assume a one-to-one mapping between a submission and a WHCC order.
- `order.tracking.available_on_ship` -- Shipment details for a WHCC order appear once that order reaches order_shipped. Treat the WHCC order's own status as authoritative for whether it has shipped: in the rare case that a carrier reports a shipment without detail, a shipped order can carry no shipment details at all. Absence therefore means no shipment details have been reported, which is almost always because the order has not shipped yet.
- `card.redirect.complete_missing_editor_id_token` -- The redirects.complete url sent with this request contains no per-item marker, so every card or album you send to this url comes back to the same place. To tell which item completed, put your own correlation key (for example your order or line id) in the url you send, or include the %EDITOR_ID% token, which for card and album items is substituted with that item's configuredProductId.
- `submission.pricing.destination_required_for_full_total` -- No shipping address was supplied, so no destination is assumed: shipping, salesTax, the US MN/CO retail delivery fee and the Canada import surtax are omitted rather than defaulted or reported as zero. totalPrice reflects product, packaging, discount, surcharges and minimumSurcharge only -- it is a product-only subtotal, not a checkout total. Supply shipping.address to receive the full breakdown.
- `design.correlation.product_ids_index_envelope` -- Several of your requested product references can resolve to the same global product, so a design's productIds can carry more than one id. Index the response's products envelope by every id in productIds, not just the first.
- `submission.pricing.value_includes_tax` -- totalPrice.value includes tax; totalPrice.total.value is the pre-tax amount. Bill the customer totalPrice.value.

autoApproveOn.description: Timestamp of when order will be auto approved.

submitOrder.description: If not specified, defaults to `true`. If `requiresApproval` has been set, the order will not be submitted.

BrokenRules.description: The rules the entry broke, when the refusal is a rule failure.

string.description: A custom size in inches, sent together with `size: "custom"`. Either axis may be the longer one; `orientation` is derived from whichever one you sent. Priced at the nearest available size at or above it, reported back as `price.pricedAs` when that is larger than what you sent.

Model16.description: Caller-supplied key/value metadata for this item. Absent or null means an empty map.

priceBasis.description: Which price is charged: wholesale or retail. A line's own value wins over the cart's; a line without one takes the cart's, and a cart without one means wholesale. Immutable once set. In this release it is recorded only and does not change the price.

input.description: The Basic Order editors[] entry this item stands for. Shape-validated only; nothing is priced or resolved until submit.

editorId.description: Id of the editor to order

editorUserId.description: Id of the user who created the editor. Omit it for API-key callers: it defaults to the token account, and naming a different account returns 403.

whccAccountId.description: Id of the account for whom this order will be submitted under (i.e. the photographer). For API-key callers -- partner API keys and browser-login sessions alike -- omit it: it defaults to the account the token is bound to, which for a browser-login session is the organization you signed into. Sending that same account is accepted; naming any other account returns 403, and an explicit empty string returns 400.

quantity.description: If excluded, take quantity from the editor

cachedUnitPrice.description: Supplied unit price, which may be used if checksum matches. Some products are always re-priced, so a matching checksum does not guarantee this price.

checksum.description: MD5 checksum of the order item

Model17.description: A single cart item: an ordering wrapper (label/quantity/metadata/priceBasis) around one Basic Order editors[] entry.

label.description: Short caller-supplied label for this item.

quantity.description: How many of this item to order. Defaults to 1. At most 10000.

items.description: Batch of items to add. At least 1, at most 100.

size.description: Deprecated form; use width and height directly instead

batchIndex.description: This photo's index in its batch

updatedDate.description: Unix timestamp at which the photo was re-uploaded (same as batchCreatedDate for now)

id.description: ID of photo; will be auto-generated if omitted

url.description: Web address to retrieve photo from

name.description: Short name for photo; derived from url if omitted

fileSize.description: Number of bytes in the file (derived by accessing the url if omitted)
